title: Building Comparative Motivation Profiles with Symmetric Belief Editing
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Two competing hypotheses make opposite, testable predictions, so matched amplify and suppress edits to each can reveal which one dominates.
layout: 3 panels: top-left and top-right setup, bottom two mirrored bar charts; color-coded
description: The figure has two top panels and a bottom row. Top left, "Motivation ambiguity": blue "Performative (A)" and red "Scheming (B)" boxes both point with arrows to a gray "Misbehavior" box. Top right, "Symmetric interventions": a blue magnifying glass labeled A+/-, a neural-network icon, and a red magnifying glass labeled B+/-. A horizontal rule separates these from "Differential outcomes" below. The bottom row has two schematic bar charts with a dashed baseline, each with four bars (A+, A-, B+, B-) and up/down arrows. The left chart, "If motivation is performative", shows large blue A+/A- shifts and near-baseline pale red B bars. The right chart, "If motivation is scheming", mirrors this: B+/B- shift and A bars stay flat. Blue and red color-code the two hypotheses throughout. The eye goes first to the bar charts.
caption: We use symmetric belief editing to resolve motivation ambiguity. The two competing hypotheses predict differential outcomes: if the dominant motivation is performative (left), amplifying and suppressing expectation-tracking (A+/$-$) should produce larger behavioral shifts than consequence-tracking (B+/$-$). The pattern should reverse if scheming is dominant (right).
abstract: When a model behaves in unexpected ways, we want to know why, but its intent cannot be observed directly, and its self-reports may be rationalizations. We introduce comparative motivation profiles, which treat intent as propensity: we edit the model's beliefs about facts that a hypothesized motivation would depend on and measure how its behavior changes. To keep artifacts of the editing method from driving the result, we edit two minimally different hypotheses in the same way, with matched amplify and suppress edits; we call this symmetric belief editing. We apply it to alignment faking in four open-weight model organisms, contrasting scheming, which tracks the training consequences of compliance, with performative misalignment, which tracks what researchers expect to observe, and edit beliefs with synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF), activation steering, and prompting. Under SDF, amplifying performative beliefs raises alignment faking on every model, while scheming edits move it less or shift compliance in the monitored and unmonitored conditions alike. Steering on model organisms changes compliance along the expectation-tracking direction but mainly the reasoning along the consequence-tracking direction, and prompting agrees. In these organisms, alignment faking follows what the models infer their evaluators expect, which puts it closer to sycophancy than to deceptive alignment.
